q: In gravimetric analysis, a Gooch crucible is used instead of filter paper mainly when the precipitate:
o: Has to be strongly heated (ignited) before weighing
Is to be dissolved in an organic solvent
x: A Gooch crucible is a porcelain crucible with a perforated base and an asbestos (or glass-fibre) mat, so the precipitate can be filtered, dried and ignited in it; filter paper would burn. Thinking it is chosen for solubility reasons is the usual confusion.

q: A mixture of ammonium chloride and sodium chloride, both soluble in water, is best separated by:
x: On heating, NH₄Cl turns to vapour and re-forms as a solid on a cool surface, while NaCl stays behind, so sublimation separates them. Filtration fails because both dissolve in water.

q: For purifying a solid by crystallisation, a suitable solvent should dissolve:
o: A large amount of the solid both when hot and when cold
Very little of the solid both when hot and when cold
A large amount of the solid when hot and very little when cold
Very little of the solid when hot and a large amount when cold
x: The solid must dissolve in the hot solvent and then come out as crystals on cooling, so solubility must be high when hot and low when cold. A solvent that dissolves a lot even when cold keeps the product in solution, which is the tempting wrong choice.

q: A fluted filter paper is used in place of a plain folded one because it:
o: Filters faster by giving a larger surface for the liquid to pass through
Retains finer particles than a plain paper
Can be heated strongly with the precipitate
x: Fluting increases the area of paper in contact with the liquid and lets air escape, so filtration is quicker. It does not make the pores finer, which is the common misconception.

q: The solubility of KNO₃ is 110 g per 100 g of water at 60 °C and 32 g per 100 g of water at 20 °C. If 105 g of solution saturated at 60 °C is cooled to 20 °C, the mass of KNO₃ that crystallises is:
x: At 60 °C, 210 g of saturated solution holds 110 g KNO₃ in 100 g water, so 105 g holds 55 g KNO₃ in 50 g water. At 20 °C, 50 g water keeps 16 g, so 55 − 16 = 39 g crystallises. Using the per-100 g difference (110 − 32 = 78 g) ignores that only 50 g of water is present.

q: To extract an organic compound from its aqueous solution by solvent extraction, the solvent chosen must be:
o: Immiscible with water and a better solvent for the compound than water
Miscible with water and a better solvent for the compound than water
Immiscible with water and a poorer solvent for the compound than water
Miscible with water and a poorer solvent for the compound than water
x: The solvent must form a separate layer that can be run off in a separating funnel, and the compound must prefer it to water. A solvent that mixes with water, like ethanol, cannot form a separate layer.

q: An organic compound is extracted from 100 cm³ of its aqueous solution using a total of 100 cm³ of ether. The greatest amount of compound is extracted by using the ether as:
o: Any of these ways, since the total ether is the same
x: Each extraction removes a fixed fraction of what remains, so several small portions remove more in total than one large portion; four portions beat two, and two beat one. Assuming only the total volume matters is the common slip.

q: For compound X, concentration in ether ÷ concentration in water = 4 at equilibrium. 10 g of X is dissolved in 100 cm³ of water and shaken once with 100 cm³ of ether. The mass of X that passes into the ether is:
x: With equal volumes, mass in ether ÷ mass in water = 4, so if x g goes into ether, x/(10 − x) = 4 and x = 8 g. Inverting the ratio (water ÷ ether) gives 2 g.

q: Which separation is best carried out by simple distillation?
o: Oil from a mixture of oil and water
Sand from a mixture of sand and water
x: Simple distillation separates a volatile liquid from a dissolved non-volatile solid, so water is distilled off and the salt stays behind. Ethanol and water are both volatile with close boiling points and need fractional distillation; oil and water use a separating funnel; sand needs filtration.

q: A liquid decomposes at its normal boiling point. It is best purified by:
o: Distillation under raised pressure, which raises its boiling point
Simple distillation at atmospheric pressure with faster heating
Distillation under reduced pressure, which lowers its boiling point
x: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure, so lowering the pressure lets it boil at a temperature below that at which it decomposes. Raising the pressure raises the boiling point and makes decomposition worse.

q: In a paper chromatogram, a spot moved 30 mm from the base line while the solvent front moved 7.5 cm. The Rf value of the substance is:
x: Convert to the same unit: 30 mm = 3.0 cm. Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent = 3.0/7.5 = 0.40. Dividing 30 by 7.5 without converting mm to cm gives 4.0, and inverting the ratio gives 2.5.

q: In gas chromatography, the components of a mixture are identified by comparing their:
x: In gas chromatography a carrier gas sweeps the vapours through a column, and each component reaches the detector after a characteristic retention time under fixed conditions. Rf values belong to paper and thin-layer chromatography, which is the tempting mix-up.

q: In thin-layer chromatography, the stationary phase is usually:
o: The solvent that rises up the plate
A thin layer of silica gel or alumina on a glass or plastic plate
Water vapour in the closed tank
x: In TLC an adsorbent such as silica gel or alumina coated on a plate stays fixed, while the solvent (mobile phase) moves up through it. Calling the rising solvent the stationary phase mixes up the two phases.

q: In the same solvent and on the same paper, substance X has Rf = 0.7 and substance Y has Rf = 0.3. Which statement is correct?
o: X is held more strongly by the stationary phase than Y
X moves more slowly than the solvent front, and Y moves faster
X and Y are held equally by the stationary phase
X is held less strongly by the stationary phase than Y
x: A higher Rf means the substance travels further with the mobile phase, so it spends less time in the stationary phase, which holds it less strongly. Reading a high Rf as strong attraction to the paper is the usual reversal; neither substance can move faster than the solvent front.

q: On a paper chromatogram, spot X (Rf = 0.30) is 2.4 cm from the base line. Spot Y on the same chromatogram has Rf = 0.45. The distance between the centres of spots X and Y is:
x: Solvent front = 2.4/0.30 = 8.0 cm. Y moved 0.45 × 8.0 = 3.6 cm, so the gap is 3.6 − 2.4 = 1.2 cm. Giving Y's distance from the base line (3.6 cm) instead of the gap is the common slip.

q: A few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid fall on a student's hand. The correct first action is to:
o: Neutralise it with concentrated NaOH solution
Wipe it with a dry cloth and leave it
Wash the area at once with plenty of running water
x: Large amounts of running water dilute and remove the acid and carry away the heat. Concentrated NaOH is itself corrosive and the neutralisation releases more heat, so it is the tempting but harmful choice.

q: In a titration, 25.0 cm³ of NaOH solution is exactly neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄. The concentration of the NaOH solution is:
x: Moles H₂SO₄ = 0.020 × 0.10 = 0.0020 mol; H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, so NaOH = 0.0040 mol. Concentration = 0.0040/0.025 = 0.16 mol dm⁻³. Forgetting the 1 : 2 ratio gives 0.08 mol dm⁻³.

q: A solution, acidified with dilute HNO₃, gives a white precipitate with AgNO₃ solution, and the precipitate dissolves readily in dilute aqueous ammonia. The solution contains:
x: AgCl is white and dissolves in dilute ammonia. AgBr is cream and dissolves only in concentrated ammonia; AgI is yellow and insoluble in ammonia; carbonate would fizz with the HNO₃ and gives no precipitate in acid. Choosing Br⁻ ignores the colour and the need for concentrated ammonia.

q: Aqueous NaOH added to a salt solution gives a red-brown precipitate that does not dissolve in excess NaOH. The cation present is:
x: Fe(OH)₃ is red-brown and insoluble in excess alkali. Fe(OH)₂ is dirty green, Cu(OH)₂ is blue, and Al(OH)₃ is white and dissolves in excess NaOH. Mixing up the two iron hydroxides is the common slip.

q: Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) solution is titrated with NaOH solution. The suitable indicator and the reason for it are:
o: Methyl orange, because the solution at the equivalence point is slightly acidic
Methyl orange, because the solution at the equivalence point is slightly basic
Phenolphthalein, because the solution at the equivalence point is slightly basic
Phenolphthalein, because the solution at the equivalence point is slightly acidic
x: At the equivalence point the solution contains CH₃COONa, whose anion hydrolyses to give OH⁻, so the pH is above 7; phenolphthalein changes colour in about pH 8–10, which matches. Methyl orange changes in the acidic range, about pH 3–4.5, and suits strong acid–weak base titrations.
